# Correlations Among Few-Body Nuclear Observables and Their Extension to Nuclear Matter

## Introduction to Established Correlations

The nuclear physics literature has long recognized the existence of remarkable correlations among low-energy observables in few-nucleon systems. Perhaps the most celebrated of these is the Tjon line, which establishes a nearly linear relationship between the triton binding energy and the alpha-particle (four-nucleon) binding energy across a wide range of nuclear interaction models. This correlation has proven to be a powerful tool for constraining nuclear forces, as it demonstrates that once realistic two-nucleon interactions are supplemented with three-nucleon forces to reproduce the triton binding energy, the four-body binding energy becomes largely determined regardless of the specific details of the underlying interaction model. In this work, we extend this well-established paradigm beyond the traditional three- and four-nucleon systems to encompass a broader class of nuclear systems, including light nuclei with larger mass numbers and, notably, infinite nuclear matter.

## Scaling Relationship for Light Nuclei

We present compelling evidence that the binding energies of light nuclei follow a scaling relationship anchored to the triton binding energy. This extension suggests that the correlation observed between three- and four-body systems is not an isolated phenomenon restricted to the lightest nuclei, but rather reflects a more general underlying feature of nuclear interactions. By systematically examining calculations performed with various realistic nuclear Hamiltonians—incorporating both two- and three-nucleon force components—we demonstrate that the binding energies per nucleon of light nuclei exhibit a consistent trend when plotted against the triton binding energy. This scaling behavior indicates that the triton, as the simplest system sensitive to three-nucleon force effects, serves as a sensitive and predictive benchmark for the binding properties of more complex nuclear systems.

## Connection to Nuclear Matter Saturation Properties

Building upon this scaling relationship, we argue that the fundamental saturation properties of nuclear matter—specifically the saturation energy and saturation density—are themselves correlated with the triton binding energy. This represents a significant conceptual extension, as it links the bulk properties of the infinite many-body system directly to a well-defined few-body observable. The physical motivation for this connection lies in the common sensitivity of both systems to the strength and structure of the three-nucleon force: just as the triton binding energy calibrates the three-body force contribution needed to reproduce experimental data in the few-body sector, this same three-body force component plays a crucial role in determining where nuclear matter saturates. The saturation point, characterized by its energy per particle and density, thus emerges not as an independent nuclear matter property, but as one intimately tied to the same physics that governs the light nuclear systems.

## Evidence from Systematic Nuclear Matter Calculations

To substantiate this proposed correlation, we draw upon systematic nuclear matter calculations available throughout the literature, spanning diverse many-body approaches and nuclear force parametrizations. When the saturation energy and density predictions from these varied calculations are compiled and analyzed collectively, a coherent pattern emerges: rather than being randomly scattered, the results appear to organize themselves into a band-like structure in the relevant parameter space. This banding suggests that the correlation with the triton binding energy is not merely a mathematical coincidence, but reflects genuine underlying physics connecting the few-body and many-body nuclear regimes. The existence of such a band structure, emerging from calculations performed independently by different groups using different methods, lends considerable credibility to the notion that a robust correlation exists linking the microscopic few-nucleon sector to the macroscopic saturation properties of nuclear matter.

## Significance and Outlook

Taken together, these findings suggest a unifying thread running through nuclear systems of vastly different sizes—from the three-nucleon triton to infinite nuclear matter. The extension of Tjon-line-type correlations across this broad range of systems implies that a relatively small set of few-body observables may encode essential information about the nuclear force that propagates through to determine the properties of much larger and more complex nuclear systems. This has important implications for nuclear theory, as it suggests that improving our understanding and precision in few-body calculations—particularly regarding the triton binding energy and the associated three-nucleon force—could yield corresponding improvements in our ability to predict and understand the saturation properties of nuclear matter, with consequences extending to the physics of neutron stars and other dense nuclear environments.

# Extending Few-Body Correlations to Nuclear Matter: From the Tjon Line to Saturation Properties

## Introduction

The study of correlations among low-energy observables in few-nucleon systems has long provided valuable insight into the nature of nuclear forces. Perhaps the most celebrated of these is the Tjon line, which establishes a nearly linear correlation between the binding energies of the three-nucleon (triton) and four-nucleon (alpha particle) systems when computed using a variety of realistic nuclear interactions. This correlation, first identified decades ago, demonstrates that despite significant variations in the details of different nucleon-nucleon potentials, the binding energies of light nuclei remain constrained by an underlying relationship that appears largely independent of the specific dynamical input. Such correlations—often referred to as Tjon-line-type correlations—have since been recognized as a general feature connecting few-body observables, and their existence raises the natural question of whether analogous relationships persist as one moves toward heavier nuclear systems and, ultimately, to the properties of infinite nuclear matter.

## Extending the Framework to Light Nuclei and Nuclear Matter

In this study, we extend the investigation of these correlations beyond the traditional three- and four-body sector to encompass light nuclei with mass numbers beyond A=4, as well as the bulk properties of nuclear matter. Our primary goal is to determine whether the binding energies of light nuclei exhibit scaling behavior analogous to the Tjon line when correlated with the triton binding energy, and whether such correlations can be meaningfully extended to describe the saturation properties of nuclear matter—namely the saturation energy and saturation density.

To this end, we perform systematic calculations of binding energies for a range of light nuclei using various realistic and chiral nuclear interactions, examining how these binding energies scale with the triton binding energy computed under the same interaction models. This approach allows us to test the universality of the Tjon-line-type correlation across an expanded range of nuclear systems, providing a broader empirical foundation for understanding how few-body observables constrain many-body nuclear properties.

In parallel, we carry out extensive nuclear matter calculations using established many-body methods, exploring how the saturation energy and saturation density vary as functions of the underlying two- and three-nucleon interactions. By correlating these saturation properties with the corresponding triton binding energies obtained from the same set of interactions, we investigate whether an analogous correlation—reminiscent of the Tjon line—manifests itself in the transition from few-body to many-body nuclear systems.

## Results and Discussion

Our analysis reveals that both the saturation energy and saturation density of nuclear matter display a clear correlation with the triton binding energy. This finding is significant, as it suggests that the same underlying physics responsible for the few-body Tjon-line correlation continues to influence the bulk properties of nuclear matter, despite the enormous increase in system complexity when moving from three nucleons to an infinite many-body system.

Furthermore, our systematic calculations indicate that the correlation is not represented by a single sharp line, as is approximately the case for the original Tjon line, but rather by a band structure. This band reflects the residual dependence of nuclear matter saturation properties on additional details of the nuclear interaction beyond what is captured solely by the triton binding energy, while still preserving an overall correlated trend. The existence of this band structure suggests that while the triton binding energy serves as a robust and physically meaningful parameter for constraining nuclear matter properties, additional degrees of freedom in the nuclear force—particularly related to three-body and higher-order effects—introduce a spread around a central correlated trajectory.

## Implications

These results provide new and valuable insight into the deep connection between few-body and many-body nuclear physics. They demonstrate that observables as fundamental as the triton binding energy, historically used to constrain and benchmark few-nucleon interactions, retain predictive power when extended to the saturation properties of infinite nuclear matter. This connection reinforces the idea that the nuclear force possesses an intrinsic set of correlations that persist across vastly different length and mass scales, from few-nucleon systems to the bulk properties of nuclear matter relevant to astrophysical objects such as neutron stars.

Moreover, the identification of a band structure rather than a single well-defined correlation line opens new avenues for future research. It suggests that a more detailed characterization of this band—potentially incorporating additional few-body observables or interaction properties—could yield tighter constraints on nuclear matter properties, thereby improving our understanding of the equation of state and its dependence on fundamental nuclear interactions. Such insights are particularly relevant for ab initio approaches to nuclear structure and reactions, where establishing reliable links between microscopic nuclear forces and macroscopic nuclear matter properties remains an outstanding challenge.

## Conclusion

This study successfully extends the well-established Tjon-line correlation from the three- and four-nucleon systems to a broader class of light nuclei and to the saturation properties of nuclear matter. The observed correlation between the triton binding energy and nuclear matter saturation energy and density, manifesting as a band structure in systematic calculations, offers a compelling new perspective on the relationship between few-body and many-body nuclear phenomena. These findings not only deepen our theoretical understanding of nuclear forces but also provide practical guidance for constraining nuclear matter properties using few-body observables, with implications extending from nuclear structure theory to astrophysical applications.

# The Tjon Evidence

The case had remained unsolved for nearly a decade before the Tjon evidence surfaced, changing everything investigators thought they knew about the events of that autumn night.

Detective Maria Santos had reviewed the file countless times, memorizing every detail of witness statements, forensic reports, and timeline reconstructions. Yet something had always felt incomplete, as if a crucial piece of the puzzle remained hidden in plain sight. The breakthrough came when a routine records request unearthed documentation that had been misfiled for years—correspondence and physical evidence connected to a man named Peter Tjon, a name that had appeared only peripherally in earlier investigations.

The Tjon evidence consisted of several elements: handwritten notes, financial records, and a set of photographs that placed Tjon at locations investigators had previously overlooked. What made this discovery particularly significant was not merely its existence, but the way it contradicted several assumptions the original investigation had made. Witnesses who had been dismissed as unreliable suddenly gained credibility. Timelines that seemed contradictory now aligned perfectly.

Legal experts debated the admissibility and weight of this evidence extensively. Some argued that the delay in its discovery raised questions about chain of custody and reliability. Others maintained that the internal consistency of the Tjon evidence, corroborated by independent sources, made it among the most compelling material to emerge in the case's history.

For the victims' families, the Tjon evidence represented something beyond legal technicality—it offered the possibility of answers long denied to them. Whether it would ultimately prove sufficient to secure a conviction or exoneration remained uncertain, but its emergence undeniably shifted the trajectory of a case many had considered permanently closed.

The story of how evidence surfaces, sometimes years after the fact, reminds us that justice systems must remain open to revisiting conclusions when new information emerges, however inconvenient that reconsideration might be.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

The Tjon line—a well-known correlation between the triton binding energy and the deuteron-triton effective range parameters, or more generally between three- and four-body binding energies—has long served as a diagnostic tool for testing the consistency of nuclear interaction models in few-body systems. In this work, we investigate whether analogous correlations persist and extend into the regime of light and medium-mass nuclei, and ultimately into the bulk saturation properties of infinite nuclear matter. Using a broad set of nucleon-nucleon and three-nucleon interactions derived from chiral effective field theory at varying orders and regularization schemes, together with phenomenological potentials, we perform systematic ab initio calculations of binding energies and radii for nuclei ranging from A=3 to medium-mass systems, alongside coupled-cluster and many-body perturbation theory calculations of the nuclear matter equation of state. We demonstrate that a Tjon-line-like linear correlation persists when comparing few-body binding energies to nuclear matter saturation density and energy, indicating that the same short-range and tensor-force dynamics governing the triton-alpha correlation propagate coherently into bulk nuclear properties. This correlation is shown to be remarkably robust across different chiral orders, cutoff choices, and fitting protocols, suggesting a universal underlying mechanism tied to the short-distance behavior of the nuclear force rather than to details of the many-body method employed. We further explore the implications of this extended Tjon-line behavior for constraining three-nucleon force parameters using few-body observables, thereby providing an efficient pathway to improve predictions for nuclear matter saturation density and energy, symmetry energy slope, and neutron star crust properties without requiring computationally expensive many-body calculations for every candidate interaction. Our findings establish a unified correlation structure connecting microscopic few-nucleon physics to macroscopic nuclear and astrophysical observables, offering new insight into the emergence of nuclear saturation from fundamental two- and three-body forces and providing a practical benchmark for the continued refinement of chiral nuclear interactions.

# Abstract

The correlation between the triton binding energy and nuclear matter saturation properties represents a longstanding benchmark for testing the reliability of nucleon-nucleon (NN) interactions derived from chiral effective field theory and phenomenological potentials. In this work, we examine the extent to which realistic two- and three-nucleon forces, when fit to reproduce two-body scattering data and the deuteron binding energy, constrain the saturation energy and density of symmetric nuclear matter through the well-established Tjon line correlation. Using a range of chiral and phenomenological NN+3N interactions, we compute the triton binding energy via Faddeev-Yakubovsky equations and the nuclear matter equation of state via many-body perturbation theory and coupled-cluster techniques. Our results confirm a robust linear correlation between the triton binding energy and the nuclear matter saturation point, extending the traditional Tjon line—originally established for two-nucleon forces alone—into the regime where three-nucleon forces are explicitly included. We find that interactions reproducing the empirical triton binding energy of 8.48 MeV systematically yield saturation densities and energies in closer agreement with the empirical point (ρ₀ ≈ 0.16 fm⁻³, E/A ≈ -16 MeV) than those calibrated to few-body data alone without 3N force constraints. This suggests that the Tjon line, when generalized to include many-body forces, serves not only as a diagnostic for few-body physics but also as a powerful predictive tool for bulk nuclear matter properties. We discuss the theoretical origin of this correlation in terms of short- and intermediate-range interaction components, and its implications for constraining next-generation chiral NN+3N+4N interactions used in ab initio calculations of medium-mass nuclei and neutron star matter.

# Abstract

Correlations among few-body nuclear observables and their extension to bulk nuclear matter properties provide a powerful probe of the underlying nuclear interaction and its renormalization scale dependence. The Tjon line—a nearly linear correlation between the triton and alpha-particle binding energies—exemplifies how few-nucleon systems computed with different two-body potentials, fit to identical NN scattering data, nonetheless exhibit systematic deviations traceable to variations in three-body (and higher) forces. This work examines the extent to which such correlations persist and generalize across the nuclear chart, linking light-nuclei binding energy systematics to saturation properties of infinite nuclear matter, including the equilibrium density, binding energy per nucleon, and incompressibility.

Using chiral effective field theory interactions evolved via similarity renormalization group (SRG) techniques, we analyze the scale and scheme dependence of these correlations, demonstrating that Tjon-line-type relations persist across a range of resolution scales, with the residual dependence on three-nucleon forces acting as a common thread linking few- and many-body observables. We show that these correlations can be exploited to constrain three-body force parameters using few-body data, thereby improving predictions for nuclear matter saturation properties. The results underscore the utility of scaling relations as diagnostic tools for assessing the consistency and predictive power of nuclear Hamiltonians derived from chiral effective field theory, and suggest pathways toward a unified description connecting few-body nuclear physics to the equation of state of nuclear matter relevant for neutron star modeling.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

The saturation properties of symmetric nuclear matter—namely the equilibrium density and binding energy per nucleon—remain among the most challenging quantities to reproduce simultaneously from realistic nucleon-nucleon (NN) interactions in ab initio many-body calculations. Despite decades of effort, calculations employing modern high-precision two-body potentials, whether phenomenological or derived from chiral effective field theory, systematically fail to reproduce the empirical saturation point, instead tracing out a well-known correlation band (the "Coester line" and its extensions) in the energy-density plane. In this work we investigate the origin of this systematic behavior by examining the connection between nuclear matter saturation and the triton binding energy, a fundamental few-body observable governed by the same underlying NN and three-nucleon (3N) dynamics. Using a broad set of interaction models spanning a wide range of off-shell behavior, tensor force strength, and short-range structure, we perform coupled calculations of the triton binding energy and nuclear matter equation of state within consistent many-body frameworks. We find that predictions for the two observables are strongly correlated: interactions yielding a more strongly bound triton systematically produce nuclear matter saturation points that are shifted toward higher density and greater binding energy, tracing out a band structure analogous to the Tjon line long established for three- and four-nucleon systems. This correlation persists across different many-body methods and interaction classes, indicating that it reflects a genuine dynamical link between two- and few-body correlations and the bulk saturation mechanism, rather than an artifact of any particular truncation scheme. We show that the inclusion of 3N forces, calibrated to reproduce the empirical triton binding energy, correspondingly shifts the nuclear matter saturation point along this band, bringing it into closer agreement with empirical saturation properties. These results establish the triton binding energy as a robust and computationally economical constraint on the nuclear force model relevant to bulk nuclear matter properties, and suggest that residual discrepancies in reproducing simultaneous saturation and triton observables point to genuine deficiencies in the two- and three-nucleon interaction models rather than to many-body truncation errors. We discuss the implications of this correlation for the systematic construction and calibration of nuclear interactions, including chiral effective field theory forces, and for reducing theoretical uncertainties in ab initio predictions of nuclear matter and finite nuclei.

# Abstract

The empirical correlation between the triton and alpha-particle binding energies, known as the Tjon line, reflects a deep connection between few-nucleon observables that emerges from the nonperturbative structure of the nuclear interaction. In this work, we investigate the extension of such correlation patterns beyond the traditional three- and four-body sector, exploring their persistence and evolution across a broader range of light nuclei and, ultimately, into the many-body limit of infinite nuclear matter. Using a set of *ab initio* few- and many-body methods applied to a family of chiral effective field theory interactions spanning a physically motivated range of low-energy constants, we systematically examine binding energies, radii, and saturation properties as functions of the triton binding energy, treated as the primary low-energy scale controlling nuclear observables. We find that Tjon-line-like correlations extend robustly to p-shell nuclei and to the nuclear matter equation of state, with the saturation density and energy per particle exhibiting approximately linear correlations with the triton binding energy, analogous to the original three-to-four-body relation. These results support the notion that the triton binding energy encodes essential information about the strength and range of the nuclear force relevant across vastly different mass scales, providing a unifying organizing principle for nuclear observables. We discuss the microscopic origin of these correlations in terms of the interplay between two- and three-nucleon forces, and we highlight their implications for constraining nuclear interactions, reducing theoretical uncertainties in *ab initio* calculations, and connecting finite-nuclei observables to the properties of dense nucleonic matter relevant for neutron stars.
